---
title: "Zone Running: Inside Zone, Outside Zone, Split Zone, and the Cutback"
subtitle: "Why five linemen step the same way at the snap, and how the running back finds a hole nobody drew"
description: "Zone blocking from the ground up: the covered/uncovered rules, inside zone, outside (wide) zone, stretch, split zone, the bash/insert/arc tags, the running back's bang-bend-bounce read, the cutback and the cut block, how defenses fight zone, why wide zone pairs with the bootleg, and what the numbers say."
glossary:
  "Zone blocking": "A blocking scheme in which every lineman steps the same direction and blocks whoever enters his area, rather than a defender named before the snap."
  "Inside zone": "A zone run aimed at the play-side guard or B gap, in which double teams drive the defensive linemen back and the running back reads for a crease, often cutting back."
  "Outside zone": {def: "A zone run aimed at or just outside the tight end, in which the line steps laterally to get the defense running sideways and the back makes one cut into the first crease.", aliases: ["Wide zone"]}
  "Stretch": "The widest zone track, aimed outside the tight end toward the sideline, whose first intent is to get the edge; in some playbooks simply another name for outside zone."
  "Split zone": "Inside zone with a tight end or H-back crossing behind the line to kick out the backside end, who would otherwise be left unblocked."
  "Bash": "Short for 'back away': a zone tag in which the running back runs away from the line's zone flow while the quarterback reads the end man and can keep the ball on the inside-zone track."
  "Insert (zone insert)": "A zone tag in which a fullback, H-back or tight end leads up through a gap to block a linebacker, adding a blocker at the point of attack."
  "Arc block": "A tight end or H-back's release around the outside of an unblocked end to block the next defender out (an overhang or safety), usually paired with a quarterback read."
  "Aiming point": "The spot a running back's first steps point at on a designed run, such as the play-side guard's outside hip on inside zone or the tight end's outside leg on outside zone."
  "Bang-bend-bounce": "The zone runner's three choices after pressing the aiming point: hit the designed gap (bang), cut back against the flow behind the blocks (bend), or take it outside (bounce)."
  "Cutback": "A ball carrier's cut against the flow of the play, back toward the side the line stepped away from, into a lane created by defenders over-running the play."
  "Backside cut-off": "The job of the linemen away from the play on a zone run: get in front of the defenders on their side so those defenders cannot chase the play from behind."
  "Cut block": "A legal block aimed at a defender's thighs or below, from the front, to put him on the ground; restricted by rule to protect knees and banned when combined with a high block (a chop block)."
  "One-cut runner": "A running back who presses the aiming point, makes a single decisive cut and goes straight upfield, rather than dancing or bouncing around in the backfield."
  "Reach-and-overtake": "A two-man outside-zone block: the play-side lineman of the pair gets his hands on a defender to stop him running wide, his neighbor races flat to take the defender over, and the first lineman climbs to a linebacker."

import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, RegularPolygon
from gridiron import (Play, Player, Field, offense, technique, style, show_animation)

OL_NAMES = {"LT": "LT", "LG": "LG", "C": "C", "RG": "RG", "RT": "RT"}
ZONE_GREEN = "#0f7a55"   # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]  # a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange


def named_line(players):
    """Label the five offensive linemen so the reader can follow each one."""
    return [p.moved(label=OL_NAMES[p.key]) if p.key in OL_NAMES else p for p in players]


def ace_condensed():
    """12 personnel: two in-line tight ends (Y right, U left), both receivers off the ball in tight splits."""
    off = named_line(offense("ace"))
    return [q.moved(w=-9.0) if q.key == "X" else (q.moved(w=9.0) if q.key == "Z" else q) for q in off]


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def secondary(cb_w=15.0):
    """Two corners and two deep safeties (a two-high shell)."""
    sw = min(9.0, cb_w - 1.5)
    return [D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -cb_w, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, cb_w, "CB"),
            D("FS", "FS", 11.5, -sw, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 11.5, sw, "SS")]


def even_front(playside=1, sam_w=6.6, cb_w=15.0):
    """A generic four-man even front (named in 05-02), linemen labelled by technique number:
    5-technique, 1-technique, 3-technique, 5-technique, three linebackers, two deep safeties.
    playside=+1 puts the 1-technique on the play side (the offense's right)."""
    s = playside
    return [
        D("PE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", s), "5"),     # play-side end
        D("PT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", s), "1"),     # play-side tackle, shaded on the center
        D("BT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", -s), "3"),    # backside 3-technique
        D("BE", "DE", 1.0, technique("5", -s), "5"),    # backside end
        D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, s * sam_w, "S"),
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, s * 1.6, "M"),
        D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -s * 2.6, "W"),
    ] + secondary(cb_w)


def front7(playside=1):
    return [q for q in even_front(playside) if q.key in ("PE", "PT", "BT", "BE", "SAM", "MIKE", "WILL")]


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, path or run."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def branch(fld, p, pts, color=style.THIRD, label=None, label_at=None, lw=2.0, fontsize=8,
           dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow"):
    """A dashed 'option' path through absolute (d, w) points, with an arrowhead (or block tee)."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    if end == "arrow":
        fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6, solid_capstyle="round")
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=11, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=6))
    else:  # a block: dashed line ending in a T-bar
        fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6)
        v = np.array([xs[-1] - xs[-2], ys[-1] - ys[-2]])
        perp = np.array([-v[1], v[0]]) / np.linalg.norm(v) * 0.75
        fld.ax.plot([xs[-1] - perp[0], xs[-1] + perp[0]], [ys[-1] - perp[1], ys[-1] + perp[1]],
                    color=color, lw=lw + 0.6, zorder=6)
    if label:
        x, y = _P(fld, p, *(label_at or pts[-1]))
        fld.ax.text(x, y, label, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, fontweight="bold", ha="center",
                    va="center", zorder=9,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=color, lw=0.8))


def overtake(fld, p, key, via, end, color=ZONE_GREEN, lw=2.4):
    """An overtake block (dashed green, T-bar end) from `key`'s alignment through `via` to `end`."""
    q = p.players[key]
    branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), *via, end], color=color, end="tee", lw=lw)


def pair_oval(fld, p, d, w, width, height=2.5, color=ZONE_GREEN):
    """A faint oval around a double team (two blockers and their defender)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), width, height, fc=color, alpha=0.24, ec="none", zorder=1.5))
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), width, height, fc="none", ec=color, lw=1.8,
                             ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=1.6))


def spot(fld, p, d, w, color=style.THIRD):
    """Mark an aiming point with an X."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=9, color=color, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=9)


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.5, ha="center"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=7),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def clean(ax):
    """Box-zoomed diagrams: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip anything outside the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:   # yard numbers, not technique labels
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=5.8, ax=None, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page, cleaned for a box-sized window."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    return fld


def play_arrow(fld, p, d, w0, w1, text):
    """A broad 'the play goes this way' arrow at depth d, from w0 to w1."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d, w0), _P(fld, p, d, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=16,
                                     color=style.OFFENSE, lw=2.2, zorder=3))
    xm, ym = _P(fld, p, d + 0.9, (w0 + w1) / 2)
    fld.ax.text(xm, ym, text, fontsize=7.5, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, ha="center", va="center", zorder=4,
                fontweight="bold")


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


MARK_R = 0.6      # frame-strip marker radius in yards: smaller than the static diagrams, so engaged
                  # blockers and defenders (about a yard apart) stay separate in print


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=(), down=None):
    """One moment of a simulated play on `ax`: markers, trails of on-screen players, rings, cut fades."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.4, play.los + window[1] - 0.4)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.4, yhi - 0.4)]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")
                & df["x"].between(play.los + window[0], play.los + window[1])]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):        # trails only for players in the panel
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    downed = [k for k, t_down in (down or {}).items() if t >= t_down]
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        if r["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.45), 0.7, 0.42, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=9))
            continue
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            gone = r["displayName"] in downed            # cut to the ground: faded, under the blockers
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon(
                (x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT,
                ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=6 if gone else 8, alpha=0.4 if gone else 1.0))
            tc = style.MUTED if gone else style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.8 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.6)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold",
                zorder=10 if tc != style.MUTED else 6.5)
    for key, col in rings:
        r = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.05, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    if downed:                                           # one "cut" tag beside them (backside)
        rr = cur[cur["displayName"].isin(downed)]
        x, y = fld.xy(rr["x"].mean(), rr["y"].max())
        ax.text(float(x) - 0.9, float(y), "cut", fontsize=7, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, ha="right",
                va="center", fontweight="bold", zorder=12,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
    return fld


def strip(play, times, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-8, 13), ncols=3, notes=None, rings=(("RB", style.THIRD),),
          down=None, title=None, width_in=6.5):
    """Frame strip with a fixed, box-sized window so markers stay legible in print.
    rings: players to circle in every frame; down: {key: t} players cut to the ground from time t."""
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.36 if notes else 0.2))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, down)
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.2f} s".rstrip("0")),
                     fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                    fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK)
    if title:
        fig.suptitle(title, x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.3 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-8, 13), rings=(("RB", style.THIRD),),
          down=None, width_in=5.6):
    """Web version of the strip: the same panel drawn at every frame, with the strip's notes as captions
    (each note shows from its frame's time on), the rings and the cut fades."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, down)
        txt = ("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s")
        if notes:
            cur = [n for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
            txt += ("   " + cur[-1]) if cur else ""
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=9, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=sorted(df["frameId"].unique()), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def zone_animation(play, times, notes=None, **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(play, times, notes=notes, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        video(play, times, notes=notes, **kw)
```

Second-and-7, early in the second quarter. The offense lines up with two tight ends, and at
the snap all five offensive linemen take the same step to their right, in unison, like a
chorus line. The running back takes the handoff on a tight path toward the right tight end,
and for a moment it looks like he is going to be swallowed by a pile of bodies. Then he plants
his foot, cuts back to the left, and runs through a hole near the center that was not there
half a second earlier. Twelve yards. The announcer says "great vision." He is right, but it
is not the whole story. That hole was not luck and the cut was not improvised. The play was
*built* to produce it. This chapter shows you how.

**You'll be able to:**

- Explain the three zone rules (step play-side, covered or uncovered, double-team and climb to the
  linebackers) and apply them to a front you have never seen.
- Tell inside zone, outside zone, stretch and split zone apart on a broadcast from the
  running back's aiming point and the line's first steps.
- Recognize the three common tags (insert, arc and bash) and say what each one adds.
- Call the running back's choice on every zone run (bang, bend or bounce) and explain
  why he made it.
- Explain the cutback, the backside cut-off and the cut block, and why the cut block is
  controversial.
- Explain why outside zone and the bootleg are a matched pair, and read a rushing-efficiency
  chart by run location without being fooled by it.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[The Language of the Run Game](03-01-run-game-language.qmd)**: gaps (A, B, C, D outward
  from the center), technique numbers for where a defensive lineman lines up (a **5-technique**
  is on the tackle's outside shoulder, a **3-technique** on the guard's outside shoulder, a
  **1-technique** shaded on the center), *covered* and *uncovered* linemen, *play-side* and
  *backside*, and the core blocks: reach, cut-off, combo (double team) and kick-out.
- **[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)**:
  [EPA](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) (expected points added: how much a
  play changed the offense's expected score) and
  [success rate](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) (the share of plays with
  positive EPA). You need these only for the numbers section near the end.
:::

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares. *Left* and
*right* always mean the offense's left and right. On offense, LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the five
linemen, Q the quarterback and R the running back. **Y** is the main tight end, lined up on
the line. **U** is a *second* tight end, on the left; zone teams love two-tight-end sets partly because
the U gives the backside a blocker, as you will see. **H** is
the "move" player from [02-02](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd):
a slot receiver in some pictures, an off-the-ball tight end (an H-back) in others, and each caption
says which. X and Z are wide receivers. On defense, linemen are labelled by technique number,
S, M and W are the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, CB is a cornerback, and FS and SS are the
safeties. Lines ending in a short bar are blocks, arrows are paths, and the thick dark arrow is
the ball carrier.

## Why block an area instead of a man?

Start with the problem zone blocking solves. On a classic "man" (or *gap*) blocking run,
the coach draws the play against the front he expects: the right guard blocks *that*
defensive tackle, the tight end blocks *that* end. That works beautifully until the defense
moves. Defensive linemen do not stand still. They [slant](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)
(step sideways into a different gap at the snap), they stunt (two linemen swap gaps), and linebackers blitz into gaps the play
assumed would be empty. A blocker assigned to a man who has just left becomes a spectator,
and the man who arrived in his place is unblocked.

[**Zone blocking**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-blocking) flips the question. Instead of
"which defender is mine?", each lineman asks "who comes into my area?" Every lineman steps the
same direction at the snap, and whoever enters the space he is responsible for is his man. If
the defensive tackle slants away, the guard simply keeps moving and picks up whoever
replaced him.

Notice what zone blocking is *not*. Linemen are not blocking "grass." They block people, every
time. What changes is *how* each lineman decides who that person is: by a rule applied after
the snap, not by a name written on the play card.

That rule-based design has a second consequence that makes zone runs feel different to watch.
Because nobody knows before the snap exactly where the hole will be, **the running back has to
find it**. The line's job is to create a moving wall and get the defense flowing sideways; the
back's job is to read where that wall cracks. A zone run is half a blocking scheme and half a
running back's decision. You will see both halves in this chapter.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Zone blocking exists because defenses move. Assigning blockers to *areas* by rule means a slant,
a stunt or a late shift does not leave a defender unblocked by surprise, the way it can when
blockers are assigned to *names*. That is a promise about assignments, not about winning: a
defender who moves fast enough can still beat his blocker physically, and you will see later
which kinds of movement hurt zone most. The price of the scheme: zone blocks are rarely knock-down,
drive-him-five-yards blocks. Zone teams accept "get in the way and keep moving" in exchange for
never losing track of a defender. And because the hole is not fixed, the play depends on a running
back who can read it.
:::

[Gap schemes](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) (power, counter and their relatives) are the other
great family of run plays and make the opposite trade, a fixed hole with extra blockers pulled to
it. Most NFL teams run both; 03-03 covers when coaches choose which.

## The three rules: step, covered or uncovered, climb

Every zone play, inside or outside, runs on the same three rules. Learn these and you can
draw a zone play against any front.

**Rule 1: everyone steps play-side.** At the snap, all five linemen (and the tight ends)
take their first step toward the side the play is going. On a broadcast this is the single
clearest tell of a zone run: the whole line moves *the same direction together*. On a gap
run, by contrast, linemen block in different directions and at least one usually pulls.

**Rule 2: covered or uncovered decides your job.** You met these words in
[03-01](03-01-run-game-language.qmd); here is how zone teams count them. A lineman is
*covered* if a defensive lineman is **head-up on him or shaded to his play-side**, that is, sitting
in the gap he is stepping into. He blocks that man. A defender shaded to a lineman's *backside*
belongs to the neighbor on that side, not to him. A lineman with nobody head-up or play-side of
him is *uncovered*. He does not stand around: his first step is still play-side, but his hands go
to the defender in the gap on his *backside*, the man his covered neighbor is blocking, while his
eyes find the linebacker behind that defender. Coaches count this in slightly different ways
(some staffs call a lineman covered whenever anyone is shaded on him), but the pairs and the
jobs come out the same.[^rule2]

**Rule 3: double-team to the second level.** That help is the heart of zone blocking. When a
covered and an uncovered lineman both have hands on the same defensive lineman, they form a
[combo block](03-01-run-game-language.qmd) (a double team). Two men move one defensive lineman,
and while they do it both keep their eyes on the linebacker behind him. When the linebacker
commits to a gap, one of the two linemen comes off the double team and "climbs" to block him,
leaving the other to finish the defensive lineman alone. The double team gets you movement; the
climb gets you the **second level** (the linebackers).

Which of the two climbs? Usually the uncovered man, the one who started with his eyes on the
linebacker; the covered man's job is the defensive lineman, and he finishes him. *When* the
climber leaves varies by coach: in one survey of line coaches, the largest group taught linemen
to come off as soon as they saw the linebacker run over the top of the double team or underneath
it.[^combo] Come off too early and the defensive lineman splits the double team; too late and the
linebacker is already in the hole.

**Edge cases.** Three situations the rules seem not to cover come up in this chapter's pictures and
drills:

- *Two uncovered linemen side by side.* An uncovered lineman helps the covered man on his backside.
  If his backside neighbor is uncovered too, there is nobody to help, so he skips the double team and
  climbs straight to the nearest linebacker.
- *The last man on the play side, with a defender outside him* (a tight end with an end lined up on
  his outside shoulder). He is covered, and there is no play-side neighbor to help him, so he has to
  block that man alone. That is the hardest block in zone, and it changes where the play hits.
- *The last man on the backside, with a defender outside him.* Nobody needs to reach a backside
  defender; the job on the backside is to stop chasers. So the last backside blocker steps inside and
  protects the gap inside him (coaches call it **hinging**, swinging shut like a door), and the man
  outside him is left to the quarterback's fake or read. That outside man is the "unblocked backside
  end" you will meet again and again.

The front in the next few pictures is a common four-man *even front*: four defensive linemen, none
of them head-up on the center. Its name and its variations belong to the defense's side of the
book, in [05-02](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-02-even-fronts.qmd); here it is just a
front to practise on.

Work through @fig-zone-rules from left to right, play going right. The left tackle's
play-side gap is the B gap between him and the left guard, and the 3-technique sits in it: the
LT is covered. The left guard has nobody head-up on him and nobody in his play-side gap (the A gap
to his right): he is uncovered, so he helps the LT on the 3-technique and looks for the Will
linebacker. The center has the 1-technique in his play-side gap: covered. The right guard is
uncovered, so he helps the center and looks for the Mike. The right tackle has the 5-technique
in his play-side gap: covered. The tight end is uncovered, so he helps the right tackle on the
5-technique and looks for the Sam.

Two things are worth noticing. First, the rules found three natural double teams (LT and LG on
the 3, C and RG on the 1, RT and Y on the 5) without the coach drawing them; a different front
would produce different pairs from the same rules, which is exactly the point. Line coaches give
these pairs short code names so two linemen can tell each other "we're together on this one"
before the snap; the names vary by staff. Second, **the defender who lines up farthest
from the play on the backside, the left 5-technique, is not on anyone's list.** Zone plays
almost always leave someone unblocked on the backside. Much of this chapter is about how the
offense deals with him.

Who decides all this? Before every snap the center usually identifies the front out loud and
makes a "Mike" call: he points out one linebacker and names him the Mike *for this play*, so all five
linemen count defenders from the same starting point and nobody disagrees about which linebacker is
whose (how lines use that call in pass protection is in
[04-02](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)). The linemen then confirm their pairs
with one-word calls. When a pair gets it wrong, two linemen block the same man, or nobody blocks
one, and you see a defender in the backfield untouched at the snap.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Zone linemen just block whoever is in front of them." Not quite. A lineman whose man is directly
in front of him but *shaded to the backside* is uncovered under zone rules, because what
matters is the gap he is stepping into. That is why two linemen facing the same front can get
different jobs depending on which way the play goes, and why zone teams spend hours of practice
on "who's covered?" against every front they might see.
:::

### The payoff: movement gets picked up

Now the claim this chapter opened with, in one picture. In @fig-zone-vs-movement the defense
runs a simple pressure at the snap: the 1-technique slants from the center's right shoulder into the
gap on his left, and the Mike linebacker blitzes into the gap the 1-technique just left. On the left,
the run is blocked *by name*: the center was told "block the 1," the right guard "block the Mike."
On the right, the same run is blocked by zone rules.

The zone line did not guess the pressure; it did not have to. Each lineman's question ("who enters my
play-side gap?") is answered *after* the snap, so whatever arrives gets blocked. One coaching manual
describes exactly this case: when the defensive lineman slants into the uncovered lineman's gap, the
uncovered man simply takes him.[^slant] That is the promise zone makes. It is not a promise to win
every block, as you will see when the movement goes *with* the line instead of against it.

## Inside zone: the downhill version

[**Inside zone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-inside-zone) is the zone play that attacks the
middle of the line. The linemen take short, firm steps play-side (more forward than sideways),
the double teams try to drive the defensive linemen *backward*, and the running back aims
between the guard and tackle.

That target has a name. The [**aiming point**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-aiming-point) is
the spot the running back's first steps point at. On inside zone it is usually the play-side
guard's outside hip, the B gap (some teams teach the A gap; it varies with the team and with
whether the quarterback is under center or in the shotgun). The aiming point is not
necessarily where the back will end up. It is where he starts, so that the defense has to
respect the play-side gaps and the back can read the blocks from there.

::: {#cell-fig-inside-zone .cell execution_count=4}

p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)])                       # RT on the 5 ...

Why build a run this way? Because the double teams are where inside zone wins. Two 300-pound
men on one defensive lineman can move him, and moving the defensive tackles off the line of
scrimmage is what opens everything else. The linebackers then face an impossible choice. If a
linebacker fills the play-side B gap early, the climbing lineman meets him there and walls him
toward the sideline, and the back cuts just inside that block, into the gap the linebacker left. If he
waits, the double team is still moving his teammate backward and the back gets downhill before anyone
arrives.

**What about the unblocked backside end?** Count the box in @fig-inside-zone: six blockers (five
linemen and the tight end) against seven defenders. One defender is always left over, and inside
zone chooses the one with the longest way to go to the ball: the end farthest from the play. That
does not make him harmless. If he simply chases down the line, he can tackle a back who cuts back
toward him. After the handoff the quarterback fakes a **bootleg** (a rollout the other way, which
you will meet properly near the end of the chapter) to make him hesitate; that is the only help plain
inside zone gives against him. The H standing on that side in the picture is a slot receiver, too far
out to block him. Later sections show the ways teams deal with him: a second tight end to block him (the
U in the two-tight-end pictures), a crossing tight end to kick him out
([split zone](#split-zone-protecting-the-backside)), or the quarterback reading him and keeping the
ball, the [zone read](03-04-option-football.qmd) of 03-04.

**What inside zone gives up:** it is a grind-it-out play. It needs linemen strong enough to
move a defensive tackle with help, and when the defense wins those double teams (a big,
penetrating defensive tackle who splits the double team) the play dies in the backfield. Its
average gain is modest; its virtue is that it is *hard to make go badly*, and it sets up
everything else.

## Outside zone: get the defense running sideways

[**Outside zone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-outside-zone), also called
[**wide zone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wide-zone), has the same rules and a different
intent. Inside zone wants to move the defense *backward*; outside zone wants to move it
*sideways*. The linemen take a lateral first step (some coaches teach a "bucket step," opening the
hips and stepping slightly back to gain width) and run, trying to get their heads across the
play-side shoulder of the defender in front of them. "Head across" is literal, and it is the whole
idea of outside zone: a blocker whose helmet and shoulders are on the play-side of a defender is
standing between that defender and the ball, so the defender can only go inside, away from where the
back is heading. A blocker whose head ends up on the inside has only got in the defender's way; the
defender can still run around him toward the ball. The running back's aiming point moves out to the
**outside leg of the tight end** (or of the tackle, if there is no tight end on that side).

That difference is the one you can see from the stands, and @fig-iz-vs-oz puts the two side by side.

::: {#cell-fig-iz-vs-oz .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}

        ("Inside zone: steps go up", (1.6, 0.7), [(-4.0, 1.8), (-1.0, 2.4)], (0.0, 2.4), "aims at the\nB gap"),
        ("Outside zone: steps go across", (0.5, 1.5), [(-4.3, 2.6), (-1.4, 5.1)], (-0.2, 5.5), "aims at the\nY's outside leg")]):

    p.highlight("RB")

Two new ideas are hiding in that picture.

**The receivers' jobs.** Z **stalk-blocks** his cornerback: he runs at him as if on a route, then
breaks down, squares up and stays between the corner and the ball. X **runs his cornerback off**:
he sprints straight downfield so the corner, who cannot know it is a run yet, has to turn and run with
him, which takes him out of the play without a block.

**Reach-and-overtake.** On outside zone, a covered lineman wants to *reach* his defender: get
his head and body to the play-side of the defender so the defender is sealed inside and the
running back can get outside him. Physically, a reach is a long lateral first step to gain ground,
then a second step aimed through the defender's play-side leg, with the inside hand driving into his
chest to stop him running.[^reach] The trouble is that a defender sitting in your play-side gap
is already a step closer to the play than you are, and he is moving the same way you are: he only
has to take one step sideways to stay outside you. Reaching him alone is close to impossible. So zone teams do it in pairs: the
[**reach-and-overtake**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-reach-and-overtake). The pairs are the
same ones the rules produced for inside zone; what changes is who touches the defender first. The
*uncovered* man of the pair (here the Y beside the 5-technique, and the RG beside the 1-technique)
is already outside the defender, so he gets his hands on him first, just enough to stop him running
wide. The *covered* man (the RT, the C) races flat down the line and *overtakes* the block, getting
in front of the defender from the inside. As soon as the overtake arrives, the first lineman lets go
and climbs to the linebacker. The covered man still ends up with his own defender; his uncovered
neighbor just got there first to hold him. It is the outside-zone cousin of the inside-zone double
team: inside zone's combo goes *forward* and splits; outside zone's combo goes *sideways* and hands off.

**The backside cut-off.** Away from the play, the linemen are not trying to move anyone. Their job
is the [**backside cut-off**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-backside-cut-off): step play-side
and get in front of the defenders on their side, so those defenders cannot chase the play
down from behind. A backside defender who is cut off is out of the play even if he is never
knocked back an inch. Notice who cuts off the backside end here: the U. Against the even front in
@fig-zone-rules, nobody had that man; a second tight end gives the backside a blocker for him, which
is a big reason zone teams like two-tight-end sets. As you will see, the backside cut-off is also
what makes the cutback possible.

play, but every player's path follows the rules above.

Notice the timing. Under center, the quarterback turns and hands off several yards deep, and the
back takes a second and a half or more to reach the line. That is by design: the line needs time to
get the defense moving sideways, and the back needs time to see which way it moved. It is why a good
outside-zone back can look slow for two steps and then very fast.

### Why outside zone exists, and what it gives up

Outside zone was built to beat a defense that is bigger than you. You cannot drive a 320-pound
defensive tackle backward, but you can make him *run*, and a running defensive lineman is a
defensive lineman who is not holding his gap. Stretch the whole front laterally, and gaps open
between defenders who are moving at different speeds. Linebackers, flowing fast to stay level
with the back, over-run the play. The back only has to find one crease.

It gives up a few things in return:

- **It needs a particular kind of lineman.** Outside zone favors lighter, quicker linemen who can
  run laterally and reach, over bigger, stronger linemen who can drive straight ahead. Teams
  built around outside zone have often gone smaller on the line; the scheme shapes the roster.
- **Fast movement *with* the line hurts it.** Zone keeps every defender accounted for when the
  defense moves, but it cannot make movement harmless. A defensive lineman who slants hard toward
  the play at the snap is moving the same way as his blocker with a head start, and the blocker may
  never get his head in front of him. One who knifes straight upfield into the gap a lateral-stepping
  blocker just left is in the backfield before the block exists, and the back's track is so wide
  that he is tackled for a loss. (@fig-zone-defense, later, draws it.)
- **It is patient by design, which means it can lose yards.** The back runs sideways for a couple of
  yards before he turns upfield. When the crease never appears, the result is a loss.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden you choose "HB Stretch," a lane lights up, and you steer the back into it. On a real zone
run, nobody knows where the lane is when the play is called. The play call tells the line which
way to step and the back where to aim; the hole is created by the defense's reaction, and the back
has to *see* it at full speed. Two identical calls of outside zone can hit three different gaps.
That is not the play failing; that is the play working. The same goes for inside zone, which is not
Madden's "HB Dive": a dive goes to one numbered hole, while inside zone's hole is wherever the double
teams and the back's read put it.
:::

## Stretch: the widest track

The word [**stretch**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stretch) causes confusion because teams use
it differently. In many playbooks "stretch" is simply another name for outside zone. When coaches
distinguish them, stretch is the widest member of the family: the aiming point moves outside the
tight end, toward the numbers, and the back's first intent is to *get the edge* (the outside
boundary of the defense, where the last defender on the line stands). The blocking is the same
lateral, reach-first zone blocking; the difference is how hard the back works to get outside before
he even considers cutting up.

Why have it? Because some fronts invite it. When the defensive end lines up inside the tight end (a
**7-technique**, on the tight end's inside shoulder), the tight end is already outside him before the
snap: half the reach is done. By the rules the end belongs to the right tackle (he sits in the tackle's
play-side gap), so the uncovered tight end gets his hands on him, the tackle overtakes, and the pair can
pin him inside and win the race to the sideline. An end lined up *outside* the tight end, as in the odd
front below, is the opposite case: nobody can get outside him easily, and stretch becomes a bad bet. The Indianapolis Colts of the Peyton
Manning era made "the stretch" a signature under line coach Howard Mudd, running it with Edgerrin
James and later Joseph Addai.[^colts]
The cost is the same as outside zone's, only more so: the wider the track, the more yards the back
can lose if the edge is not there.

In this book, when a distinction matters we say *inside zone* (aimed inside), *outside zone*
(aimed at the tight end, ready to cut up), and *stretch* (aimed outside the tight end, edge first).
On a broadcast you will usually hear "outside zone" and "stretch" used interchangeably. That is
fine. Watch the aiming point and you will know which one you are seeing.

## Same play, different front: the rules re-pair

The most important thing about zone blocking is that the *same call* works against different
fronts, because the rules re-pair the blockers after the defense shows its hand. Here is the
same outside zone against an [odd front](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd),
one with a nose tackle head-up on the center (a 0-technique), two 4i-techniques (on the inside
shoulder of each tackle) and two outside linebackers on the line, each in a 9-technique (on the
tight end's outside shoulder). You will learn its name and logic in
[05-03](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd); for now it is
"a different front."

Apply the rules again (@fig-outside-zone-odd). The Y is now covered (a 9-technique sits in his
play-side gap), so he has to reach that man by himself, a hard block. The right tackle is uncovered:
the 4i lines up on his inside shoulder, which is his *backside*, so that defender belongs to the right
guard, whose play-side gap he sits in. So the RT and RG form the new reach-and-overtake pair: the RT
gets his hands on the 4i first, the RG overtakes, and the RT climbs to the Mike. The center is covered
by the nose head-up on him. The left guard is uncovered and right next to him, so he helps: the center
works to the nose's play-side half while the left guard hits the nose's backside hip, and once the
center has him, the guard climbs to the Will. The left tackle cuts off the backside 4i. The U is the
last man on the backside with a defender outside him, the third edge case from the rules: he hinges,
stepping inside to wall off anything that crashes down inside him, and the 9-technique outside him is
left alone, as the backside end was on inside zone.

::: {#cell-fig-outside-zone-odd .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def odd_front(cb_w=10.0):
    return [
        D("POLB", "OLB", 1.0, 6.0, "9"),
        D("P4i", "DE", 1.0, technique("4i", 1), "4i"),
        D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
        D("B4i", "DE", 1.0, technique("4i", -1), "4i"),
        D("BOLB", "OLB", 1.0, -6.0, "9"),
        D("MIKE", "ILB", 4.5, 2.4, "M"),
        D("WILL", "ILB", 4.5, -2.4, "W"),
    ] + secondary(cb_w)


p = Play([q for q in ace_condensed() if q.key not in ("X", "Z")], odd_front(), los=35, to_go=10,
         title="Same outside zone vs an odd front: the rules re-pair")
go_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 6.7), via=[(-0.4, 5.7)])            # reach the 9-tech alone
go_to(p, "RT", (3.4, 3.0), via=[(0.5, 2.4)])            # hands on the 4i, climb to the Mike

Compare the two pictures and you will see what coaches mean when they say "the front tells
you where the play will hit." Against the even front, the hardest block was the overtake on the
1-technique, and the edge was reachable. Against this odd front, the two hardest blocks are the
center and left guard on a nose head-up on the center, and the tight end on a man lined up outside
him. If the 9-technique cannot be reached, the back will not bounce. He will hit it up inside him,
or cut back. The rules did not change. The *likely hole* did.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
A zone play is really a *set of rules*, not a drawing. Rules let one play call adapt to every front
the defense can show, which is why zone teams can run a handful of plays all game without being
predictable in the way that matters: the defense knows the call, but not where the ball will hit.
Defenses fight back with fronts and movement that put the offense's weakest blocker in the
hardest job, a story you will pick up in [Part 5](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-02-even-fronts.qmd).
:::

**Who picks inside or outside zone, and which way?** The play-caller, from the sideline, as with every
call (01-05). But the line of scrimmage still gets a vote. Many offenses let the quarterback flip a run to
the other side (a [kill call](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-kill-call)), or check out of it into a pass, when the defense's alignment makes the called side a bad bet,
for example when it shows more defenders in the box than the offense can block. How much freedom he has
varies a great deal by team; the [pre-snap chapter](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) covers how
checks work.

## The runner's half: bang, bend, bounce

Now the other half of the play. The zone back's job is to take the handoff, **press** the aiming
point (run at it hard enough that the defense believes the ball is going there), read the
blocks, and choose. Coaches compress the choice into three words:
[**bang-bend-bounce**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bang-bend-bounce).

- **Bang**: hit the designed gap and go straight upfield. The blocks went as drawn.
- **Bend**: cut back against the flow, behind the double teams, usually into the backside A or B gap.
  The defense flowed too fast, and the space is behind them.
- **Bounce**: take it outside. The edge defender got pinned inside, and the corner is open.

The order matters, and it is different for the two plays.

On **inside zone** the back thinks *bang, bend, bounce*. He reads the first defensive lineman
play-side of the center, the man the first double team is working on. Why that man? Because he sits
right next to the aiming point, and what happens to him answers both questions at once: if the double
team is moving him, the play-side gap beside him is open; if he is sliding toward the play to get in
front of it, he is taking the space behind him out of play for the defense, and the linebackers behind
him usually flow the same way. One defender tells the back where the defense is going. If that defender is
walled off and there is daylight beside him, bang. If he (and the linebackers behind him)
flowed hard to the play-side, there is space behind them: bend. Bounce is the last resort on
inside zone, because running outside on a play built to go inside usually means running away
from your blockers. It is the right answer only when the play-side end has crashed inside and
nobody has stayed outside to take his place.

On **outside zone** the order flips to *bounce, bang, bend*, and the back makes two reads in
order. His **first read** is the play-side end, the first defensive lineman outside the tackle:
is he reached? Remember who ends up with him: the reach-and-overtake pair, with the right tackle taking
him over from the tight end. If the end is slow, or plays inside, and the tackle gets his head across
him and pins him inside, the edge is open: bounce. That is uncommon against a good end lined up outside
the tackle, which is why most outside-zone runs end up as bang or bend. If the end fights hard to stay
outside, the tackle rides him wider and the back moves to his **second read**, the next
defensive lineman inside, and asks where the hole is relative to *him*. If that man has been walled
off, there is a crease between him and the end: bang, up inside the end. If he and the linebackers
are racing to the sideline, the space is back the other way: bend, which on outside zone often
becomes a full cutback (next section). The second read is the one to watch if you want to see a
cutback coming.

Coaches teach this read in slightly different words and keys (some read a linebacker rather
than a lineman), and you should expect that variety.[^bbb] The principle under all of them is the
same: **press, read, then make one cut.**

For your own log, keep the boundary simple: **bang** if the back crosses the line in the play-side
gaps, **bounce** if he goes outside the play-side end, **bend** if he comes back against the flow.
Every bend is a cutback; the big ones that carry him outside the backside tackle are what
broadcasters mean by "he found the cutback."

That last phrase of the principle describes a style. A [**one-cut runner**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-one-cut-runner)
presses the aiming point with patience, plants one foot, and goes straight upfield; he does not
dance, stutter or reverse field behind the line. Zone coaches prize this style above raw speed,
because a zone run's creases are open for a fraction of a second and close quickly. A back who
hesitates or takes two cuts arrives after the hole has closed. It is why zone teams have often won
with backs drafted in late rounds or signed off other teams' rosters: the scheme rewards
decisiveness and vision more than it rewards a top-10 pick's raw talent. (The 1990s Broncos are
the classic example; see below.)

## The cutback and the backside

Here is the play from the chapter's opening: second-and-7, two tight ends, the line steps right in
unison, the back runs at the right tight end, plants, and comes back through a hole near the center.

A [**cutback**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cutback) is a cut *against* the flow of the play,
back toward the side the line stepped away from. On outside zone it is not a desperation move.
It is one of the three answers the play was designed to produce. Here is why it works. When eleven
defenders see five linemen and a running back all racing to their right, they race to their right
too. Linebackers who are taught to stay level with the ball carrier take aggressive angles, and a
fast defense can over-run the play: everyone ends up play-side of the ball. The space behind them is
empty, *as long as the backside defenders cannot get there first*.

That condition is what the [backside cut-off](#outside-zone-get-the-defense-running-sideways) is
for. The backside linemen do not need to move anyone; they need the defensive linemen on their side
to be on the ground, turned around, or walled away from the cutback lane. When they succeed, the
cutback is the most explosive play in the zone family, because the back runs into space that the
defense vacated on purpose.

The opening play: the cutback (simulated play). The linebackers and the play-side defensive tackle (the 1) over-run the outside zone. On the backside, the LT and the U cut their defenders to the ground (faded, tagged 'cut' from frame 2), so nobody is left to close the backside. The back (ringed) presses the tight end's outside leg, sees no room, plants, and cuts back through the backside A gap, beside the center; only the deep safety is left to make the tackle.
:::
:::


::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The cutback is the running back freelancing." It is the opposite. The back is following the
play's own logic: press the aiming point to pull the defense one way, then take the space the
defense left. Zone coaches often say the back should *expect* to cut back on outside zone, and
coach the backside linemen as if the ball will come their way. A back who never cuts back makes
outside zone easy to defend, because the defense can then over-pursue for free.
:::

### New block: the cut block

To clear a cutback lane quickly, backside linemen often do not try to stand a defender up. They
cut him. A [**cut block**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cut-block) is a block aimed at a
defender's thighs or lower legs, from the front, to put him on the ground. A defender on the ground
cannot chase, and for a lighter zone lineman facing a heavier defensive tackle who is trying to run
down the line, a cut is often the most reliable way to take him out of the play. "From the front"
matters, because the backside defender is running *sideways*, chasing the play: the blocker's
play-side step puts him in front of that path, so the defender runs into the block instead of being
hit from behind or the side.

It is also the most controversial block in football, because a block at the knees can end a career.
The NFL has narrowed it again and again: low blocks are now legal only near the ball, inside the
"tight end box" around the line; never from behind or from the side while moving back toward your
own goal line (since 2013); and never combined with a high block by a teammate, the
[chop block](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd),
banned in every situation since 2016.[^cutrule] The details are in
[09-03](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd).
Mike Shanahan's Denver lines were criticized for years for backside cuts; in 2004, after a Broncos
lineman's cut block broke a Bengals defensive tackle's ankle on *Monday Night Football*, opposing
head coaches and the broadcast crew criticized the team publicly.[^cutcrit] Defenders call it dirty;
zone coaches call it legal technique that lets small linemen block big ones. With the rules this much
tighter, how often a modern line cuts on the backside depends on its line coach. When you do see a
backside defensive tackle go down at the snap on a zone run, you have probably just seen one.

## Split zone: protecting the backside

Back to inside zone's unblocked backside end, the man who can chase down a cutback. [**Split
zone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-split-zone) takes him away.

::: {#cell-fig-split-zone .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB", "RB")] + [
    Player("Y", "TE", "off", -0.7, 4.8, label="Y"),
    Player("H", "TE", "off", -1.3, 6.4, label="H"),       # off-ball TE ("H-back") on the right
    Player("X", "WR", "off", -0.7, -11.0, label="X"),
    Player("Z", "WR", "off", -1.5, 11.0, label="Z"),
]
off = [q.moved(w=-1.6) if q.key == "RB" else q for q in off]
p = Play(off, even_front(+1, cb_w=11.5), los=35, to_go=10,
         title="Split zone: the H kicks out the backside end")
p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)])
p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)])
p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)])
p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
go_to(p, "H", (0.3, -3.7), via=[(-1.8, 4.6), (-1.8, -2.6)])  # just behind the heels: kick out the end
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 2.3), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.2)])      # cross the QB's face to the B gap
go_to(p, "QB", (-5.5, -1.6), "path", speed=3.0)              # mesh, then fake a keep away
p.handoff("RB", t=0.7)
p.highlight("H"); p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-13, 13), window=(-8, 13))
spot(fld, p, 0.0, 2.4)
branch(fld, p, [(-1.4, 2.3), (-2.6, 0.6), (-1.9, -0.8), (0.6, -0.9), (2.6, -0.6), (6.6, 0.4)],
       color=ZONE_GREEN, label="bend", label_at=(7.6, 0.6))
say(fld, p, -3.6, -8.0, "H crosses just behind\nthe line, kicks out the end", fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -6.8, 4.0, "back crosses\nthe QB's face", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()

The H (an off-the-ball tight end) runs the other way, just behind the linemen's heels and in front of the handoff, and kicks out the backside end. With that end blocked, the back's bend lane (dashed green) runs between the double team on the 1 and the left guard's block on the Will.](03-02-zone-running_files/figure-html/fig-split-zone-output-1.svg){#fig-split-zone}

The line blocks exactly as it would on inside zone. The difference is one man: an H-back or
tight end, lined up off the ball on the play-side, who at the snap runs *across* the formation,
just behind the linemen's heels and in front of the handoff, and [kicks out](03-01-run-game-language.qmd)
the backside end. The name comes from the picture: the play "splits," with the line and the back
going one way and the H going the other.

**Under center or in the shotgun.** Every picture before this one put the quarterback under center,
where he turns his back to the defense, hands off and fakes the other way; turning away hides the ball
and puts him in position to carry out the fake. From the shotgun, where most NFL snaps happen, the back
usually lines up beside the quarterback and on inside zone runs *across* the quarterback's face at
the handoff: a back offset to the left usually runs inside zone to the right. That gives him a
running start toward the aiming point and keeps the exchange (the **mesh**, the moment the ball
changes hands; not the pass concept of the same name in
[04-04](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)) moving downhill. Defenses know this tendency, so offenses break it on purpose with
*same-side zone* (the back runs to the side he lined up on) and with the
[pistol](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd), where the back
stands directly behind the quarterback and his alignment says nothing about direction.

**Why it exists.** Split zone solves three problems at once. It blocks the one defender plain inside
zone leaves free. It protects the cutback, so the back can bend without an end waiting for him.
And the H's path is misdirection: a linebacker who keys the H (follows his movement to find the play)
takes a false step the wrong way. It also builds a family. The same H motion across the formation is
the action for bootlegs and for passes to the H in the [flat](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)
(the short area near the sideline, within a few yards of the line), so the defense cannot simply crash
on the H's path.

**What it costs.** The H is no longer available to block play-side, so the play-side is one blocker
lighter than it could be. If the defense brings an extra defender to the play-side, split zone can be
outnumbered there. Every zone variation is this kind of trade: put a blocker where the threat is,
and accept that he is not somewhere else.

## Tags: insert, arc and bash

Zone teams rarely change the line's rules. Instead they add a [tag](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), a word added to the play
call that changes one or two players' jobs (you met tags in
[01-04](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)). Three zone tags are worth knowing,
because you will see all three on Sundays.

::: {#cell-fig-zone-tags .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))

# insert
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("singleback")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "Y", "QB", "RB")]
off.append(Player("H", "TE", "off", -4.4, -1.8, label="H"))            # offset fullback
p = Play(off, front7(), los=35, to_go=None)
p.block("C", pts=[(1.1, 0.6)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(1.0, -0.7)])      # the double stays on the 1
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)]); p.block("Y", pts=[(0.6, -0.6), (3.6, 1.5)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (3.7, 1.8), via=[(-2.6, 0.6), (0.3, 2.3)])                 # insert on the Mike
p.run("RB", [(3.0, 1.0), (6.0, 2.7), (10.0, 3.0)], delay=0.25)
p.highlight("H")
f = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=(-7.5, 8.5), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
point_to(f, p, (-6.2, -4.6), (-4.4, -1.8), "H: offset\nfullback", fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (-4.2, 5.4), (0.6, 1.0), "double team\nstays on the 1", fontsize=6.8, color=ZONE_GREEN)
axes[0].set_title("Insert: H leads up on the Mike", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")

# arc
off = [q for q in named_line(offense("gun_2x2")) if q.key in (*OL_NAMES, "QB")]
off += [Player("H", "TE", "off", -1.5, -6.6, label="H"), Player("RB", "RB", "off", -5.0, -1.6, label="R")]
dfn = [q for q in front7() if q.key != "SAM"] + [D("SS", "SS", 5.0, -9.6, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.block("C", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)]); p.block("RG", pts=[(0.8, -0.8), (4.3, -0.4)])
p.block("RT", pts=[(0.9, 0.6)])
p.block("LT", pts=[(0.9, 0.7)]); p.block("LG", pts=[(0.8, -0.6), (4.3, -0.8)])
go_to(p, "H", (4.1, -9.3), via=[(0.4, -7.6), (2.6, -9.0)])               # arc past the end to the safety
go_to(p, "RB", (1.0, 2.6), "run", via=[(-4.0, -0.4), (-1.4, 2.3)])       # give: inside zone right
p.read("BE")
p.highlight("H"); p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=(-12, 4.0), window=(-8, 6.5), title=False)
branch(f, p, [(-5.0, 0.0), (-4.4, -2.0), (-2.6, -4.4), (-0.4, -5.4), (4.0, -6.2)], label="keep",
       label_at=(5.4, -6.0), fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-3.4, 2.8), (-1.4, 2.3), "give", fontsize=7, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-6.6, -9.0), (1.0, -4.0), "read end:\nnot blocked", fontsize=6.8, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
axes[1].set_title("Arc: H runs past the end", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

:::

**Insert.** On [**insert**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-insert-zone-insert) (or "zone insert"),
a fullback, H-back or tight end leads up through a gap and blocks a linebacker, usually the play-side
one (some staffs insert on the backside linebacker instead). That frees the play-side double team
from having to climb: it can stay on the defensive lineman longer and move him farther. In effect,
insert adds a blocker at the point of attack, which is how a zone team answers a defense that keeps
one more defender in the [box](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) than
the offense has blockers. The cost is the usual one: the inserting player is not available as a
receiver, and his alignment (an offset fullback, or a tight end off the ball) can tip the play.

The other two tags borrow an idea from [option football](03-04-option-football.qmd), which gets its
own chapter: instead of blocking the unblocked backside end, the quarterback *reads* him (watches
what he does after the snap) and decides whether to hand the ball off or keep it. For now, all you
need is that idea; 03-04 builds it properly.

**Arc.** Arc happens on the *backside*, away from the line's flow. The line zones right and the back
runs inside zone to the right, while on the left a tight end or H-back makes an
[**arc block**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-arc-block): he releases outside the unblocked
backside end, runs past him without touching him, and blocks the *next* defender out, the linebacker or
safety responsible for the alley between the end and the sideline (the
[alley player](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd) of Part 5). The
quarterback reads the end. If the end stays home, the quarterback gives and the back runs inside zone.
If the end chases the running back down the line, the quarterback keeps, runs around the end the other
way, and finds the arc block already waiting for the next man. Arc is why you sometimes see a tight end
run right past a defensive end without touching him: he was never supposed to.

Bash needs one more step of background. On the standard **zone read** (03-04 draws it), the back runs
the inside-zone track and the quarterback, reading the backside end, keeps the ball around that end if
the end chases the back. Defenses learned an answer: the end crashes down hard at the back, inviting the
keep, while a linebacker loops around behind him to meet the quarterback where he was about to run (a
**scrape exchange**: the end and the linebacker swap jobs).[^scrape] The defense's plan is a bet that the
back will be inside and the quarterback outside.

::: {#cell-fig-zone-bash .cell execution_count=13}

        ax.set_title("Zone read: back inside, QB outside", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK,

**Bash.** [**Bash**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bash) is short for "back away": the running
back runs *away* from the direction the line is zoning, on a wide path around the read end, while
the quarterback, if he keeps, runs the inside-zone track behind the line (@fig-zone-bash). It flips
the usual roles: the running back threatens the edge and the quarterback becomes the inside runner.
The read is the same end, with the answers reversed: if he *squeezes* (closes down the line toward
the zone flow), the quarterback hands the ball to the back going around him; if he stays wide to take
the back, the quarterback keeps and runs inside him.[^bash] Against a scrape exchange, that matters: the
end who crashes down to take the inside runner has crashed onto the quarterback's fake, and the ball is
going outside him with the running back. Bash is the offense's reply to the defense's reply, and the full
back-and-forth belongs to [option football](03-04-option-football.qmd).

All three tags share one logic: **keep the zone rules for the line, and change one or two players
to fix the specific problem the defense is creating.** Watch for the extra player (the inserting
back, the arcing tight end, the back running the "wrong" way) and you will usually know which tag you
are watching.

## How defenses fight zone

Zone's rules guarantee that every defender is accounted for. They do not guarantee that every block is
won, and defenses attack the places where zone is physically hardest. @fig-zone-defense shows the two
most common.

**Penetration and movement.** A defensive lineman who gets upfield at the snap, or slants hard toward
the play, can beat a lateral-stepping blocker to the spot. Defenses that want to stop zone often play
their linemen this way, attacking a gap instead of reading the man in front of them; how defensive
linemen are taught to do either is the subject of
[05-01](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd).

**The cutback player.** Because outside zone's biggest gains come from the cutback, defenses assign
someone to stay home for it: usually the backside linebacker, sometimes a safety rotating down. You
saw the deep safety arrive late in @fig-cutback; a defense that gets a defender there *early* takes away
the play's third answer.

**Spill or squeeze.** When a blocker comes at a defender, the defense chooses whether that defender
fights *inside* the block to force the ball to bounce wide toward pursuit (*spill*) or holds the edge
and squeezes the play back inside (*squeeze*). Against zone, either plan can work if all eleven
players agree on it, which is the subject of run fits in
[05-05](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).[^fits]

And when the defense simply puts more defenders in the box than the offense has blockers, a zone team
answers with the tools you have already seen: an extra blocker (insert), a read of the unblocked man
(arc, bash, the zone read), or a pass that looks like the run.

## Why wide zone and the bootleg are married

Outside zone's greatest weapon is not a run at all. It is the pass that looks exactly like it.

Think about what outside zone teaches a defense. Every snap, the line steps hard to one side, the
back runs at the tight end, and the linebackers learn that if they do not flow fast and hard, they
lose. The backside end learns that if he does not chase, the cutback beats him. After a few of
these, the defense is *trained* to run with the line's first step.

The [bootleg](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) cashes that in. It is a
[play-action](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) pass (a pass that begins
with a fake handoff) in which the quarterback fakes outside zone one way and rolls out the other,
away from where the line went, with receivers crossing the field to meet him. In the "naked" version
nobody blocks for him at all; in the protected version a lineman or a back is assigned to the backside
end. Both are built in [04-05](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd); here, what
matters is why they pair with zone.

What differs: on the boot, nobody blocks the backside end; if he chases the fake down the line onto the back's track, he ends up behind a quarterback rolling away from him, who has three receivers at three depths on the boot side: the U in the flat, the Y on a crossing route (releasing inside the play-side end) and the Z on a deep over route.](03-02-zone-running_files/figure-html/fig-zone-boot-output-1.svg){#fig-zone-boot}
:::

The two plays look identical for the first second, which is the second that decides how the
defense moves. (The "over" route is a deep crossing route: the receiver runs across the field 15 or
more yards downfield, *over* the linebackers.) On a bootleg the backside end's job is to *contain* the quarterback: stay outside him
and force him back toward the pursuit. An end who chased the run fake (as outside zone has taught him
to) is now *behind* a quarterback rolling away from him, and nobody is there to make the quarterback
hurry. The linebackers who flowed with the line are a step or two the wrong way, and the
*crossing routes* (receivers running across the field) come open behind them. The boot gives the
quarterback three receivers at three depths on the same side: a short one in the flat, one crossing
at linebacker depth, and one deep. That simple read is what makes the play so reliable.

**Why the pair works.** Each play protects the other. If the defense sits back and refuses to flow,
outside zone gets the edge or the crease. If it flows hard, the bootleg punishes the flow. And because
the two share the same first step, the defense cannot wait to find out which one it is facing. This
is the backbone of the Shanahan-family offenses you will meet in
[12-03](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd): a run game and a play-action game built
to be indistinguishable for as long as possible.

**How to tell them apart after the snap.** Three plays send a tight end or H-back at the backside
end, and before the snap they can look the same. Watch what he does when he gets there:

- He **hits** the end and drives him out: split zone.
- He runs **past** the end without touching him and blocks the *next* man out (a linebacker or safety),
  while the quarterback rides the ball with the back and watches the end: arc.
- He runs past the end into the flat and **turns to look for the ball**, while the quarterback pulls the
  ball and rolls the other way: bootleg.

**The cost.** A naked bootleg leaves the quarterback with nobody blocking the backside end. If that end
does *not* bite on the fake (if he stays home), he is waiting for a quarterback who has turned his back
to him. That is why the bootleg works only once outside zone has earned the defense's respect.

## Where zone came from

Running backs reading blocks is as old as football. Vince Lombardi's Green Bay Packers of the 1960s
ran their famous power sweep with a simple instruction to the ball carrier: run to daylight, wherever
the blocks open it, a phrase that became the title of a 1963 book Lombardi wrote with W. C.
Heinz.[^lombardi] That sweep was a gap play with pulling guards, not a zone play, but its runner's
freedom to choose the hole is the same idea zone backs live by.

Who invented zone *blocking* is disputed, and nobody serious claims a single inventor. The best-documented
claims put it in the NFL of the 1980s. Jim McNally, the Cincinnati Bengals' offensive line coach, was
one of the era's most copied line coaches, and Cincinnati's run game finished in the league's top five
every year from 1986 to 1990. McNally himself said, "I didn't invent zone blocking, but we and the
Cleveland Browns did it back in the '80s," and he described it as an answer to the rise of the 3-4
defense and its penetrating linemen. Cleveland's line coach in those years was Howard Mudd,
the same coach who later made the stretch a Colts signature.[^origins] Coaches who credit older roots
point to blocking ideas in earlier college offenses; treat any one-name "inventor" story with suspicion.

What is not in dispute is who made outside zone the identity of an NFL offense. **Alex Gibbs**, an
offensive line coach with a famously blunt teaching style and a reputation as one of the best line
coaches of his era, built the Denver Broncos' running game under head coach **Mike Shanahan** from
1995.[^gibbs] Denver had a specific problem to solve. Pittsburgh defensive coordinator Dom Capers had
popularized the *zone blitz*, in which a linebacker blitzes and a lineman drops into coverage in his
place, so the defenders a man-blocking line had assigned itself kept changing. "When you're in a man
scheme, you're getting picked off and you look bad," Gary Kubiak, then Denver's offensive coordinator,
later remembered.[^espn2019] (In blocking, "picked off" means a blocker's path is cut off by a defender
he was not assigned, so his own man runs free: exactly the left side of @fig-zone-vs-movement.) Blocking by area meant that whoever came was blocked.

Gibbs's system was close to a religion: a small number of runs, repeated until the linemen could
execute them against any front; light, quick linemen who could reach and run; backside cut blocks; and
backs taught to press the aiming point and make one cut. His clinic tapes on zone running circulated
widely among coaches and are still sold as coaching videos, and many of the phrases in this chapter
descend from his teaching.[^gibbstapes]

Denver's results became the advertisement. The Broncos won back-to-back Super Bowls after the 1997 and
1998 seasons, and running back Terrell Davis, a sixth-round draft pick, ran for 2,008 yards in 1998
and was named the league's MVP.[^davis] When injuries ended Davis's peak, Denver kept producing
1,000-yard rushers with a string of other backs, several of them mid- or late-round picks, which
convinced the league that the *scheme* was doing much of the work.[^denverbacks]

The system spread through a coaching tree. Gary Kubiak carried it to Houston as head coach and back to
Denver, where he won Super Bowl 50 after the 2015 season. Kyle Shanahan, Mike's son, coached under
Kubiak in Houston and under his father in Washington, then became the 49ers' head coach in 2017. From
Kyle Shanahan's staffs came Sean McVay (Rams), Matt LaFleur (Packers) and others, and Kubiak's son Klint
called plays for the 2025 Seattle Seahawks before becoming the Raiders' head coach for 2026.[^tree] By
late in the 2019 season, ESPN's charting found zone blocking in use by all 32 teams and on at least half
of the runs of most of them; LaFleur's Packers led the league at 70.3% of runs (same ESPN study). The tree and its
offense get a full case study in [12-03](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Denver Broncos, Super Bowl XXXII (1997 season)"}
**The game:** Super Bowl XXXII, January 25, 1998: Denver 31, Green Bay 24. Terrell Davis carried 30
times for 157 yards and three touchdowns and was named MVP, despite a migraine that blurred his vision
and kept him out of part of the second quarter.[^sb32] Coaches' film from the 1990s is hard to find, but
Super Bowl broadcasts are the easiest games of the era to track down, and this one is dominated by Gibbs's
zone running (Denver mixed in other runs and play-action too).

**What to notice:**

- The line's first step. Every lineman moves laterally together; you will seldom see a Denver guard pull.
- Davis's patience. He runs at the tight end's outside leg for two or three steps and does not cut until
  the end commits. Then he cuts once, hard, and is going north.
- The backside. Watch the defensive linemen away from the play. Many end up on the ground in the first
  second: that is the backside cut, and it is why Davis's cutbacks so often had nobody in them.
- The bootleg. John Elway faking the stretch and rolling away is the other half of the same system.
:::
